summary: Defines the syntax of the Network Access Identifier (NAI), the user identity a client submits during network authentication, to support roaming between ISPs. It revises RFC 2486 with international character set and privacy support and corrections. It is on the standards track and was later replaced by RFC 7542.

plainLanguage.summary: When someone dials in to a network they are not a customer of, the network has to work out which provider the person belongs to. This RFC defines the text form of that identity, so different providers can read it the same way.

questions: what is a network access identifier
how long can an nai be
what characters can an nai username contain
how does an nai hide the username
subtitle: The syntax for the user identity a client sends when it asks a network for access, so a roaming provider can be identified.

tldr.problem: When a user dials in to a network run by a provider they do not have a contract with, the network needs a standard way to name the user's own provider so the authentication can be routed there.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Access Identifier is a username, an at sign and a realm, written in a grammar derived from SMTP usernames and DNS domain names, with optional international character support and the option of leaving the username out.
tldr.outcome: The RFC revised RFC 2486 and added international character set and privacy support. It was later obsoleted by RFC 7542.

today: RFC 4282 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 7542, so read that document for the current rules.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
Considerable interest exists for a set of features that fit within the general category of roaming capability for network access, including dialup Internet users, Virtual Private Network usage, wireless LAN authentication, and other applications. Interested parties include regional Internet service providers looking to combine their efforts with those of other regional providers to offer dialup service over a wider area, national providers wishing to combine their operations with those of one or more providers in another nation, wireless LAN hotspots providing service to one or more providers, and businesses wishing to offer their employees a comprehensive package of dialup services on a global basis, including secure access to corporate intranets over tunnels such as PPTP, L2F, L2TP and IPsec tunnel mode.

In order to enhance the interoperability of roaming services, it is necessary to have a standardized method for identifying users, and this document defines the syntax for that identity, the Network Access Identifier (NAI). The NAI is the user identity submitted by the client during network access authentication. In roaming, its purpose is to identify the user and to assist in routing the authentication request to the right server. The NAI may not be the same as the user's e-mail address, nor the identity submitted in an application layer authentication.

The document also defines the terms it uses. The Network Access Server (NAS) is the device that clients connect to in order to get access to the network: the access concentrator in PPTP terminology, the L2TP access concentrator in L2TP terminology, and an access point in IEEE 802.11. Roaming capability is loosely defined as the ability to use any one of multiple providers while maintaining a formal customer relationship with only one. This document is a revised version of RFC 2486, with international character set and privacy support added and a number of corrections made.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone dials in to a network they are not a customer of, the network has to work out which provider the person belongs to. This RFC defines the text form of that identity, so different providers can read it the same way.

sections.title: The Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The grammar for the NAI is given in Augmented Backus-Naur Form. The grammar for the username is based on RFC 821, and the grammar for the realm is an updated version of RFC 1035:

nai = username / "@" realm / username "@" realm

The username is a dot-string of characters, where each character is either one of a permitted set of ASCII characters or an escaped character written as a backslash followed by a byte. The permitted set includes the exclamation mark, hash, dollar, percent, ampersand, apostrophe, asterisk, plus, hyphen, slash, digits, equals sign, question mark, upper and lower case letters, caret, underscore, backquote, braces, pipe and tilde. The double quote, parentheses, comma, semicolon, colon, less-than sign, greater-than sign, at sign, square brackets, backslash and DEL are not allowed. Character codes 128 to 255 are allowed as UTF-8 octets, which was not the case in RFC 2486.

The realm is one or more labels separated by dots, where a label starts with a letter or a digit and may contain letters, digits and hyphens. The grammar for the realm allows it to begin with a digit, which is not permitted by the RFC 1035 grammar, because fully qualified domain names such as 3com.com are commonly used and accepted by current software.
sections.plainLanguage: The identity is a name, an at sign and a realm, or just one of those. The name may contain letters, digits and some punctuation, and the realm looks like a domain name.

sections.title: Length and Privacy
sections.content:
Devices handling NAIs MUST support an NAI length of at least 72 octets, and support for a length of 253 octets is RECOMMENDED. NAIs are often transported in the User-Name attribute of RADIUS, which recommends handling at least 63 octets, so it may not be possible to transfer NAIs beyond 63 octets through all devices. Only a single User-Name attribute may be included in a RADIUS message and the maximum attribute length is 253 octets, so RADIUS cannot carry NAI lengths beyond 253 octets. NAIs can also be transported in the User-Name attribute of Diameter, which supports content lengths up to 2^24 - 9 octets, although an NAI transported over Diameter may eventually be translated to RADIUS, where the same limits apply.

Interpretation of the username part depends on the realm in question, so the username SHOULD be treated as opaque data by nodes that are not part of the authoritative domain for that realm. In some situations NAIs are used together with a separate authentication method that can transfer the username in a more secure manner, and in that case NAIs MAY be provided in an abbreviated form by omitting the username part. Omitting the username part is RECOMMENDED over using a fixed username part such as anonymous, because it gives an unambiguous way to determine whether the username is intended to identify a single user.
sections.plainLanguage: A device must accept an identity of at least 72 bytes, and 253 bytes is recommended. If the name is left out entirely, that is a clear signal that the name is being hidden, which is better than putting a fixed word like anonymous in its place.

sections.title: International Character Sets
sections.content:
This specification allows both international usernames and realms. International usernames are based on the use of Unicode characters, encoded as UTF-8 and processed with a certain algorithm to ensure a canonical representation. Internationalization of the realm portion of the NAI is based on IDNA.

To ensure a canonical representation, characters of the username portion MUST fulfil the ABNF in this specification as well as the requirements of the SASLprep profile: mapping requirements, which map certain characters to others such as SPACE in order to increase the likelihood of correctly performed comparisons; normalization requirements, also designed to assist in comparisons; prohibited output, since certain characters are not permitted in correctly formed strings and conformance with the ABNF alone is not sufficient; bidirectional character handling; and unassigned code points, whose use is prohibited.

The mapping, normalization and bidirectional character processing MUST be performed by end systems that take international text as input, which in a network access setting are typically the client and the AAA server. NAIs are sent over the wire in their canonical form, so tasks such as normalization do not typically need to be performed by nodes that just pass NAIs around. End systems MUST also check for prohibited output and unassigned code points, and other systems MAY do so when they know that a data item is an NAI.

The realm name is an IDN-unaware domain name slot, which means it can contain only ASCII characters. An implementation MAY support Internationalized Domain Names using the ToASCII operation. The conversion of internationalized domain names to ASCII is left to the end systems, and domain name comparisons, matching, resolution and AAA routing are expected to be performed on the ASCII versions, which provides a canonical representation and means that intermediate systems such as AAA proxies do not need to perform translations.
sections.plainLanguage: A name can contain characters from any language, as long as the sending and receiving systems put them in a standard form first, so that two spellings of the same name compare equal. The realm part stays in plain ASCII.

sections.title: Realm Construction
sections.content:
NAIs are used, among other purposes, for routing AAA transactions to the user's home realm. Usually the home realm appears in the realm portion of the NAI, but in some cases a different realm can be used, for instance when the home realm is reachable only via another mediating realm. Such usage may prevent interoperability unless the parties involved have a mutual agreement that it is allowed.

NAIs MUST NOT use a different realm than the home realm unless the sender has explicit knowledge that the specified other realm is available and that the other realm supports such usage. The sender may determine this through a database, dynamic discovery, or other means. The use of the home realm MUST be the default unless otherwise configured.

Where these conditions are fulfilled, an NAI such as user@homerealm.example.net may be represented as homerealm.example.net!user@otherrealm.example.net. The part before the non-escaped exclamation mark must be a realm name, and the realm receiving this NAI must convert the format back to user@homerealm.example.net when passing the NAI forward, as well as applying appropriate AAA routing for the transaction. The conversion may apply recursively, so an NAI with more than one exclamation mark is converted one realm at a time. This syntax is optional and is not part of the ABNF; the exclamation mark may appear in the username portion for other purposes, and in those cases the interpretation is up to an agreement between the identified user and the realm given after the at sign.
sections.plainLanguage: Usually the realm says where the person is a customer. When a network can only reach that provider through another one, the realm can be written to name the provider that should handle the request, with the real home provider named in front of it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Since an NAI reveals the home affiliation of a user, it may assist an attacker in further probing the username space. This is of most concern in protocols that transmit the username in clear text across the Internet, such as RADIUS, and protocols may use confidentiality services such as RADIUS protected by IPsec or Diameter protected by TLS.

This specification adds the possibility of hiding the username part in the NAI by omitting it, which is possible only when NAIs are used together with a separate authentication method that can transfer the username in a secure manner. Some Extensible Authentication Protocol methods apply method-specific pseudonyms in the username part of the NAI. While neither of these approaches can protect the realm part, their advantage over transport protection is that the privacy of the username is protected even through intermediate nodes such as NASes.
sections.plainLanguage: The realm in the identity says which provider the person belongs to, and that is visible to anyone who can see the traffic. The name part can be left out entirely when another method carries it securely.

viz.caption: THE NAI GRAMMAR FROM RFC 4282, SECTION 2.1

data.title: Network Access Identifier
data.code:
nai         =  username
nai         =/ "@" realm
nai         =/ username "@" realm

username    =  dot-string
dot-string  =  string
dot-string  =/ dot-string "." string
string      =  char
string      =/ string char
char        =  c
char        =/ "\" x

realm       =  1*( label "." ) label
label       =  let-dig *(ldh-str)
ldh-str     =  *( alpha / digit / "-" ) let-dig
let-dig     =  alpha / digit
